lead: The ideal-gas law, PV = nRT, is the simplest equation of state. It treats molecules as points with no attractions, so heat, work and internal-energy change follow from the path alone. Engineers use it for a first estimate of compressor duty, pipeline pressure drop or the air in a tyre, and it is the reference against which real gases are measured. This chapter fixes the sign convention and works the five common paths with numbers.
prereq: You need: P–V diagrams, and the first law, enthalpy and heat capacities from the basic concepts of thermodynamics.

sections.h3: The ideal-gas law and its energy

blocks.text: The ideal-gas law is PV = nRT, with P the absolute pressure, V the volume, n the moles and T the absolute temperature. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, or 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ when V is in L and P in bar. Never put T in °C: 25 °C is 298.15 K.

In this model molecules have no volume and no forces except elastic collisions, so U depends on T only, and so does H = U + PV = U + nRT. An isothermal change therefore has ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0 even when P and V change.
PV = nRT; C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R; γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>
blocks.where: P is absolute pressure; V is volume; n is moles; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is absolute temperature in K; C<sub>p</sub> and C<sub>v</sub> are molar heat capacities at constant pressure and volume; γ is the heat-capacity ratio.

blocks.text: Here C<sub>v</sub> = (∂U/∂T)<sub>V</sub> is the heat to raise 1 mol by 1 K at constant volume and C<sub>p</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>P</sub> the same at constant pressure. For a diatomic gas near room temperature, C<sub>v</sub> ≈ (5/2)R and C<sub>p</sub> ≈ (7/2)R, so γ ≈ 1.4; monatomic gases have γ ≈ 1.67.

sections.h3: Five paths and one sign convention

blocks.text: Use W as work done by the gas on the surroundings. Then the first law for a closed system is ΔU = Q − W. Q is heat added to the gas; W is positive for expansion and negative for compression. State this convention before any calculation.

blocks.where: ΔU is change in internal energy; Q is heat added to the gas; W is work done by the gas on the surroundings.

blocks.text: Each path fixes one quantity. Integrate W = ∫P dV along the path. The table gives closed-system results for an ideal gas with constant C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub>; ΔT = T<sub>2</sub> − T<sub>1</sub>. The work formulas are for reversible paths; for irreversible paths use the actual external pressure.

An isochoric path has no volume change, so W = 0; all heat goes into U. An isobaric path expands against constant pressure, so W = PΔV and Q = ΔH. An isothermal path keeps U and H fixed; heat and work cancel. An adiabatic path has Q = 0; work comes from U, so expansion cools the gas. Also PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant, TV<sup>γ−1</sup> = constant and TP<sup>(1−γ)/γ</sup> = constant. A polytropic path PV<sup>k</sup> = constant uses k, the polytropic exponent; it covers the range between isothermal (k = 1) and adiabatic (k = γ); for k = 1 use the isothermal formula.
Some syllabi call these non-flow processes. Flow devices such as nozzles and compressors use the steady-flow energy equation instead, with enthalpy in place of internal energy; do not mix the two.

sections.h3: Mixtures and the limit of the model

blocks.text: For a mixture of ideal gases each component obeys P<sub>i</sub>V = n<sub>i</sub>RT, with P<sub>i</sub> its partial pressure, and P = ΣP<sub>i</sub> (Dalton's law). The mixture's U and H depend on T only, and its C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub> are mole-fraction averages.

The ideal-gas law is accurate at low pressure and high temperature, when molecules are far apart. At high pressure or near condensation use the compressibility factor or a cubic equation of state; the paths here still give a first estimate.

figure.caption: Worked example 1 on a P–V plot: 1 mol at 300 K is squeezed from 24.94 L to 12.47 L. The isothermal path ends at 2.00 bar, the adiabatic path at 2.64 bar because compression heats the gas to 396 K, and the isobaric path stays at 1.00 bar because the gas is cooled to 150 K.

spec.aria: Pressure from 0 to 3 bar against volume from 10 to 26 litres. From the start point at 24.94 litres and 1 bar, a solid isothermal curve rises to 2.00 bar at 12.47 litres, a dashed adiabatic curve rises more steeply to 2.64 bar at 396 kelvin, and a flat isobaric line stays at 1.00 bar, ending at 150 kelvin.

examples.question: One mole of an ideal gas is at 300 K and 1.00 bar. Its volume is 24.94 L. It is taken to 12.47 L by three separate paths: (a) isothermal, (b) adiabatic with γ = 1.4, (c) isobaric. Find the final pressure for each path. Use R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps: Check the start: V<sub>1</sub> = nRT<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = 1 × 0.08314 × 300/1.00 = 24.94 L, as given.
(a) Isothermal: T is constant, so P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub> = (1.00 bar)(24.94 L)/(12.47 L) = 2.00 bar.

(b) Adiabatic: PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant, so P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>(V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>)<sup>γ</sup>. The volume ratio is 24.94/12.47 = 2.000. P<sub>2</sub> = (1.00 bar)(2.000)<sup>1.4</sup> = 2.64 bar. The temperature follows from TV<sup>γ−1</sup> = constant: T<sub>2</sub> = 300 × 2.000<sup>0.4</sup> = 395.9 K.
(c) Isobaric: P is fixed, P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> = 1.00 bar. Halving V at fixed P needs T to halve too: T<sub>2</sub> = 300 × 12.47/24.94 = 150 K, so heat must be removed.

Check: L cancels in each ratio and pressure stays in bar. The adiabatic pressure is the highest because compression work raises the gas temperature to 396 K with no heat let out; at the same small volume a higher T gives a higher P.
examples.answer: Final pressures: (a) 2.00 bar at 300 K, (b) 2.64 bar at 395.9 K, (c) 1.00 bar at 150 K.
examples.check:
n = 1.0
R = 0.08314
T1 = 300.0
P1 = 1.0
V2 = 12.47
gamma = 1.4
V1 = n * R * T1 / P1
P<sub>iso</sub> = P1 * V1 / V2
P<sub>ad</sub> = P1 * (V1 / V2) ** gamma
P<sub>isob</sub> = P1
print(round(P<sub>iso,</sub> 2))
print(round(P<sub>ad,</sub> 2))
print(round(P<sub>isob,</sub> 2))

examples.question: For the same three paths of worked example 1, take C<sub>v</sub> = (5/2)R = 20.785 J/(mol·K) and C<sub>p</sub> = (7/2)R = 29.099 J/(mol·K). Find W (by the gas), Q and ΔU for each path, and check ΔU = Q − W.
steps: (a) Isothermal at 300 K: W = nRT ln(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>) = 1 × 8.314 × 300 × ln 0.5 = −1728.8 J. ΔU = 0, so Q = W = −1728.8 J: the work put in leaves as heat.
(b) Adiabatic, T<sub>2</sub> = 395.85 K: Q = 0. W = nC<sub>v</sub>(T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) = 20.785 × (300 − 395.85) = −1992.3 J. ΔU = Q − W = +1992.3 J, all stored in the gas.
Heat for (c): Q = nC<sub>p</sub>ΔT = 29.099 × (150 − 300) = −4364.9 J. Energy change: ΔU = nC<sub>v</sub>ΔT = 20.785 × (−150) = −3117.8 J.
Check (c): Q − W = −4364.9 − (−1247.0) = −3117.9 J, equal to ΔU within rounding. Negative W everywhere means work is done on the gas, as expected for a compression.
examples.answer: Isothermal W = Q = −1728.8 J, ΔU = 0; adiabatic W = −1992.3 J, Q = 0, ΔU = +1992.3 J; isobaric W = −1247.0 J, Q = −4364.9 J, ΔU = −3117.8 J. The adiabatic path needs the most work.

traps: PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant is for adiabatic, not isothermal. Isothermal is PV = constant; using γ there gives a wrong final pressure.
Put T in kelvin. 27 °C is 300 K; using 27 in PV = nRT is a large error.
State the W sign convention. Many engineering texts take W by gas positive (ΔU = Q − W); many chemistry texts take W on gas positive (ΔU = Q + W). Mixing them flips Q.
For a rigid tank use C<sub>v</sub>, not C<sub>p</sub>. Q = nC<sub>v</sub>ΔT for isochoric; Q = nC<sub>p</sub>ΔT for isobaric.
Adiabatic does not mean isothermal. Q = 0, but T changes and W = nC<sub>v</sub>(T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) is not zero.

quiz.q: State the ideal-gas law and give R in both J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
quiz.a: PV = nRT; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T must be in K.

quiz.q: Why is ΔU zero for an isothermal change of an ideal gas, even when V changes?
quiz.a: Ideal-gas U depends only on T. If T is constant, U is constant, so ΔU = 0. Work is balanced by heat.

quiz.q: 1 mol of ideal gas with γ = 1.4 is compressed adiabatically and reversibly from 1.00 bar and 300 K to 5.00 bar. Find T₂.
At the same (P, V) point, which curve is steeper on a P–V diagram: isothermal or adiabatic? Give the slope reason.
quiz.a: Adiabatic is steeper. Slope is −P/V for isothermal and −γP/V for adiabatic; γ > 1, so the adiabatic slope magnitude is larger.

quiz.q: In the W-on-gas convention ΔU = Q + W, expansion work is W = −PΔV. If a student wrongly writes W = +PΔV, is the Q obtained too high or too low, and by how much? Use the correct value as reference.
quiz.a: The Q obtained is too low by 2PΔV. Correct: Q = ΔU + PΔV. With W = +PΔV the equation gives Q = ΔU − PΔV, which is 2PΔV smaller.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use the ideal-gas law as the first pass, then switch to cubic equations of state or compressibility correlations near the dew point. The same path formulas appear in compressor sizing, but with efficiency and flow terms added. Search for ideal-gas polytropic compression and compressibility-factor generalized correlation to go further.
